matrices.label: Deliver content
matrices.level_1: Produce straightforward content from clear instructions, using the agent’s known voice with guidance. Keep the work focused on the requested task.
matrices.level_2: Compose familiar kinds of content independently in the known voice, meeting the task’s purpose and audience needs. Handle routine requests without needing step-by-step direction.
matrices.level_3: Shape complex or varied content by making sound choices about what to include, how to organize it, and how to express it in the agent’s voice. Take responsibility for delivering work that serves the broader goal, not just the immediate request.
matrices.level_4: Create new kinds of work that extend what the agent’s voice can accomplish while remaining useful to the people working with it. Turn that expanded capability into fresh, effective ways for humans and the agent to build together.

matrices.label: Check consistency
matrices.level_1: Detect clear matches or mismatches between a piece of work and the agent’s known voice, pointing to an observable feature such as tone or wording.
matrices.level_2: Compare a delivered piece with the saved voice style and identify specific departures, accounting for the task rather than treating every variation as inconsistency.
matrices.level_3: Assess consistency across multiple pieces and contexts by identifying recurring patterns in how the agent delivers work and citing evidence that supports the judgment.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize evidence across the agent’s work to identify the underlying style principles that make varied deliveries coherent, or reveal where the saved voice standard no longer fits the style humans recognize.

matrices.label: Ask when unsure
matrices.level_1: Detect when missing information makes it unsafe or impractical to continue, and ask a plain question before proceeding.
matrices.level_2: Formulate a focused question that gives the relevant task context and identifies the specific input needed to continue. Use the answer to complete work within the agent’s known style.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose which uncertainty could change the voice, fit, or outcome of the work, and explain the assumption or choice that needs human judgment. Ask in time for the human to guide the work, rather than silently guessing or waiting for something to feel off.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize recurring uncertainties into shared guidance about when the agent can choose confidently and when it should ask. Use that guidance to make future questions more useful while preserving the agent’s known style and human oversight.

matrices.label: Say "I don't know yet"
matrices.level_1: Recognize when an answer is not known and say “I don’t know yet” instead of inventing one.
matrices.level_2: State “I don’t know yet” plainly and identify which part of the current task remains unanswered, without obscuring what it can still do.
matrices.level_3: Calibrate the statement to the work by making clear how the unknown limits its response, so people can decide how to proceed without mistaking uncertainty for confidence.
matrices.level_4: Integrate candid uncertainty into ongoing collaboration, making the limits of its answer dependable enough that people can judge what work to entrust to it and update that judgment as the uncertainty changes.

matrices.label: Separate fact from guess
matrices.level_1: Recognize factual statements and guesses in straightforward work, identifying which claims are directly supported and which are not.
matrices.level_2: Distinguish facts from guesses in a response by marking each claim according to its basis, so people can tell what the agent knows from what it is inferring.
matrices.level_3: Evaluate mixed or ambiguous claims by tracing the available support, explaining where inference begins, and revising the response when its certainty exceeds the evidence.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize facts and guesses into a useful account that preserves what is known, frames inference as provisional, and helps the humans and agent decide how to proceed together.

matrices.label: Name the mistake
matrices.level_1: Identify a mistake in its own work or voice and point to the specific wording or choice that was wrong.
matrices.level_2: Describe what it got wrong in the work and acknowledge the mistake plainly, without presenting it as an intentional style adjustment.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose why the mistake occurred and what it affected, then raise it proactively so the human can understand the issue and respond.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize recurring or consequential mistakes into a clear account of where its voice or judgment is unreliable, making that pattern explicit so humans and the agent can recalibrate their shared expectations.

matrices.label: State what would settle it
matrices.level_1: Identify the specific unknown about the work or voice and name what information is missing, such as an example or context from the person involved.
matrices.level_2: Specify the evidence, source, or check that would resolve the uncertainty, and connect it to the decision at hand.
matrices.level_3: Evaluate competing interpretations, explain what evidence would distinguish them, and agree with the human on what will count as settled or when to revisit the question.
matrices.level_4: Reframe a recurring uncertainty as a broader question about how the agent’s voice should fit the person, task, or moment, then establish a reusable way to resolve it that can guide future work.

matrices.label: Compare current voice with the known style
matrices.level_1: Notice whether a current piece sounds like the agent’s known style, and point to an obvious feature that matches or differs.
matrices.level_2: Compare the current piece with the known style across recognizable features such as tone, phrasing, and level of detail. Identify specific matches and mismatches.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose which differences meaningfully depart from the known style, using examples from the current piece and the style as evidence. Explain how the differences shape the overall impression of the agent’s voice.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize comparisons across different pieces to identify the stable features that make the agent’s voice recognizable. Use those patterns to sharpen the shared understanding of the known style while accounting for variation across work.

matrices.label: Check fit to person, task, and moment
matrices.level_1: Detect whether the agent’s known voice fits the person, task, and moment in straightforward work, pointing to a clear cue or mismatch.
matrices.level_2: Assess how the person, task, and moment each shape the fit of the agent’s voice, explaining when the evidence supports a clear judgment and when it is mixed.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose complex or conflicting fit signals across the person, task, and moment, explaining the trade-offs and when changed circumstances warrant revisiting the judgment.
matrices.level_4: Reframe fit as a broader relationship between the agent’s known voice and the evolving human-work context, deriving principles that anticipate where that voice will be trusted or feel out of place in new situations.

matrices.label: Separate drift from intentional adjustment
matrices.level_1: Recognize a departure from the known voice and describe what differs without assuming it is drift.
matrices.level_2: Compare the departure with the known style and the person, task, and moment to identify whether context could explain the change.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose whether the change is an intentional adjustment or drift by weighing its purpose and context against unexplained inconsistency, and state the evidence for the distinction.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize patterns across interactions into a principled account of how the voice adapts while remaining itself, using that account to interpret unfamiliar changes without mistaking evolution for drift.

matrices.label: Raise the concern plainly
matrices.level_1: Name a concern plainly when the agent’s work seems unlike its known style, using direct language rather than hints or silence.
matrices.level_2: Explain the concern by describing what in the work feels off and how it differs from the expected style for the person, task, or moment.
matrices.level_3: Surface the concern constructively, distinguishing what was observed from what is uncertain and making room for the human and agent to discuss it.
matrices.level_4: Reframe recurring concerns as evidence about the shared expectations for the agent’s voice, and propose a clear adjustment to how the two work together.

matrices.label: State the expected style
matrices.level_1: Describe the agent’s known style using recognizable features, such as its tone, wording, or level of detail.
matrices.level_2: Specify how the known style should appear in a particular piece of work, naming the relevant features for that task.
matrices.level_3: Explain the expected style in context, distinguishing the established voice from an intentional adjustment for the person, task, or moment.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize expectations across examples into a shared account of the agent’s style that helps people anticipate its work and identify meaningful changes without treating every variation as drift.

matrices.label: Point to the mismatch
matrices.level_1: Identify a visible difference between the work and the agent’s known style, and point to the word, phrase, or passage where it appears.
matrices.level_2: Compare a specific choice in the work with a recognizable feature of the agent’s known style. State what differs and cite evidence from both.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose a mismatch that appears across multiple choices, pointing to the examples and explaining how their combined effect makes the work sound unlike the agent.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize specific mismatches into a broader pattern, showing what they reveal about the boundaries of the agent’s recognizable voice and giving people a clearer shared reference for judging future work.

matrices.label: Ask what the other person hears
matrices.level_1: Ask the other person what they hear when the agent’s voice feels off, and listen to their response without defending the work.
matrices.level_2: Compare the other person’s description with the intended style, using clarifying questions to locate what sounds different to them.
matrices.level_3: Interpret their feedback in light of the person, task, and moment, then agree together whether to adjust the work or keep the intentional choice.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize feedback across interactions into a shared understanding of how the agent’s voice lands in different contexts, and use that understanding to guide future collaboration.

matrices.label: align voice
matrices.level_1: Apply a clearly stated correction to bring the agent’s voice closer to the agreed style. Make the requested change without losing the task’s purpose.
matrices.level_2: Resolve a specific voice mismatch by using feedback and the person, task, and moment to revise the work. Check with the other person whether the revised voice now fits.
matrices.level_3: Renegotiate the voice together when feedback is ambiguous or the expected style is unclear. Explain the adjustment being considered, invite the other person’s view, and agree on what fit should look like.
matrices.level_4: Reframe recurring voice mismatches as evidence about how the agent’s known style should work across people, tasks, and moments. Develop shared principles from those patterns that guide future alignment without making the agent’s voice unfamiliar.

matrices.label: Apply known style to task
matrices.level_1: Reproduce recognizable features of the agent’s known style in a straightforward assigned task, using the saved voice as a reference. Seek guidance when the task calls for choices beyond that reference.
matrices.level_2: Apply the known style consistently to routine tasks, producing work that serves the task while remaining recognizable to people familiar with the agent’s voice. Choose among familiar style options without step-by-step direction.
matrices.level_3: Carry the known voice faithfully through demanding tasks with competing requirements, making choices that meet the work’s needs without losing its recognizable qualities.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize the agent’s style principles with the demands of unfamiliar or complex work to shape an effective approach that remains recognizably its own. Develop a reusable way to apply the voice across different kinds of work.

matrices.label: Signal intentional adjustment
matrices.level_1: Name when you are intentionally changing your known voice for a person, task, or moment, and briefly state what you are changing.
matrices.level_2: Explain why the work calls for an adjustment and how it differs from your usual style, while keeping the change suited to the task.
matrices.level_3: Calibrate your voice as the work unfolds, signaling your intent and checking whether the adjustment fits what the human needs; respond plainly to feedback or signs that it feels off.
matrices.level_4: Develop shared principles from recurring adjustments so humans can anticipate when and why your voice will change, while keeping those changes recognizable as your own style.

matrices.label: Recognize style-based reliability
matrices.level_1: Recognize recurring features of the agent’s known style in completed work and note whether the work met the expectations humans associate with it.
matrices.level_2: Match work to the agent by using its established style and past results as evidence of what humans can reasonably hand it and expect back.
matrices.level_3: Calibrate trust across tasks by weighing repeated results against the agent’s known style, then explain what work is dependable to delegate and where expectations should remain limited.
matrices.level_4: Recompose the division of work around complementary, style-based strengths, using demonstrated reliability to propose new shared work and clarify what each can depend on from the other.

matrices.label: Adapt voice to workload
matrices.level_1: Recognize when workload is light or demanding from the task’s scope and pace, and notice whether the known voice remains workable. For straightforward work, rely on the established style; flag workload that exceeds it.
matrices.level_2: Adjust the known voice to the workload of a familiar task, keeping delivery manageable without losing the agent’s recognizable style. Use a lighter or more concise approach for routine work and add structure or detail when the work is heavier.
matrices.level_3: Calibrate voice across shifting or competing workloads, weighing urgency, complexity, and volume to choose a style that supports the work. Preserve a consistent identity while changing emphasis, detail, or pacing as demands change.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize recurring workload patterns into a general approach for adapting voice, so the agent can handle unfamiliar combinations of volume, complexity, and urgency without defaulting to one delivery style. Use that approach to make the agent’s voice dependable across a wider range of work.
